summary: Describes an operational technique that uses BGP communities to remotely trigger black-holing of a destination network, in order to block denial-of-service attacks. The black-holing can be applied on selected routers. It also describes a sinkhole tunnel approach.

plainLanguage.summary: When a flood of junk heads to one address, routers can be told to throw the junk away early. This document describes a way to give that order.

questions: how to block ddos with bgp
subtitle: Using BGP communities to remotely trigger traffic blocking for DDoS defense.

tldr.problem: When a network is under a denial-of-service attack, the traffic flood reaches the target before the network operator can react manually. Normal routers throughout the network keep forwarding the attack traffic.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes using BGP communities to tag networks under attack, and configuring edge routers to discard traffic matching those communities by routing it to a null interface. A refined approach applies this selectively to routers near the attack entry points.
tldr.outcome: Networks can quickly block attack traffic at multiple points without disrupting normal service elsewhere. A sinkhole tunnel variant allows traffic inspection before final disposition.

facts.label: Target address granularity
facts.value: Can be host routes (/32) or entire networks (/24, etc.)

today: RFC 3882 is Informational and describes an operational technique that remains in use. The described approach to BGP-based DDoS defense remains relevant for networks that want to rapidly deploy black-holing without complex external systems, though modern deployments may also use specialized DDoS mitigation services.

sections.title: The Problem of Distributed Denial-of-Service Attacks
sections.content:
Denial-of-service attacks send such a flood of traffic to a victim network that legitimate users cannot access services. Traditional defense requires manual intervention: a network operator must detect the attack, decide where to block it, and configure routers to drop the traffic.

The older approach changes the BGP route for the attacked network throughout the entire autonomous system (AS) by pointing the next hop to a private address that leads to a null interface. The problem is that this makes the target network unreachable to everyone, not just the attacker, and disrupts all traffic to those addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: When hackers flood a website with junk traffic, network operators used to tell all routers to throw away anything going to that website, but that blocked real visitors too.

sections.title: Targeted Black-Holing with BGP Communities
sections.content:
This RFC describes an improved technique using BGP communities to mark routes with special community values. Each border router in the AS is assigned a unique community identifier; for example, router R1 gets community 65001:1, R2 gets 65001:2, and both together get 65001:666. This allows operators to target the routers where attack traffic enters.

When an attack arrives, the network operator announces the attacked address with the appropriate community tag. Routers that match the tag apply route policies to divert only that traffic to a null interface, while other routers forward it normally. The operator must ensure routes are tagged only for traffic the AS itself generated, to prevent external BGP peers from misusing the feature.

This selective approach minimizes the impact on legitimate traffic and allows the attack defense to be applied only at the routers closest to the entry points.
sections.plainLanguage: Each border gate is labeled with a code. The network operator can tell just the gates facing the attacker to block the junk, while leaving other gates open for normal traffic.

sections.title: Sinkhole Tunnels for Attack Analysis
sections.content:
Black-holing (dropping) traffic stops the attack but provides no information about who is attacking or what they want. A sinkhole tunnel is a refinement that captures the traffic for inspection instead of just discarding it.

When a sinkhole tunnel is configured, one router is designated as a sinkhole device with a port attached for traffic analysis. Border routers are configured with tunnels (using MPLS Traffic Engineering, for instance) that redirect attacked traffic toward the sinkhole router instead of the null interface. The sinkhole router receives the traffic, logs or inspects it, then forwards legitimate-looking traffic onward to its true destination. Border routers that do not match the attack community operate normally.

This approach allows operators to understand attacks in progress while still defending against them, without making the target service unreachable.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of just throwing away the junk, a special router can catch and inspect it first, then send the good stuff through to the real destination.

sections.title: Protection Against Misuse
sections.content:
A critical security consideration is that external BGP peers (customers or partners) must not be able to use these communities to black-hole arbitrary networks. The RFC emphasizes checking that routes matching the special community are only accepted if they were locally generated (i.e., the attacked network is part of the operator's own prefix).

Implementation requires careful configuration: route policies must match both the community value and the AS path in order to permit the policy change. Without this check, an external peer could advertise any network with the special community and cause the AS to black-hole traffic to targets outside the operator's control.
sections.plainLanguage: The network must check that the blocking instruction comes from inside the network, not from attackers trying to trick it into blocking websites they want to hurt.

messages.label: Traffic discarded at null interface
messages.note: Attack traffic is dropped, legitimate traffic is sent normally from other routers
